title: Assignment 1: Models and Scripts
text:
Introductory Notes

Save Programs as Live Code .m Files
As of MATLAB R2025a, both traditional scripts (plain-text programs) and live scripts (plain-text files that include formatted text, images, output, and so on) share the .m file extension, so the extension alone does not tell you what kind of file you have.
For this course, all homework submissions must be live scripts saved using the plain-text live code format (.m). If you are unsure, use Save As in the Live Editor and confirm the file type is set to MATLAB Live Code File (UTF-8) (*.m).


Submitting Your Work
Completing assignments typically consists of writing programs (scripts, live scripts, function files, and so on). These files are submitted by uploading them to the AE2440 Sakai site under the appropriate assignment. A few things will make the submission process run smoothly.

Check your work. To ensure that your program runs in a clean workspace, before submitting your final solution execute the clear command and then run your program from an empty workspace. This helps avoid errors from undefined variables.
Exact file names. Pay particular attention to the specified file names, including letter case (programming is case-sensitive!). The file names must be exactly as requested so that any automation on the evaluation end runs without a file-not-found error.
Live scripts, include output. When submitting live scripts, first run your live script to generate all specified numeric data, figures, and so on as inline output within your text and code. Then save the file (which will include the output). This lets the instructor review your solution quickly, but also debug and re-run your code if necessary.


Verify Sakai Uploads
When you upload your files to Sakai, take an extra step to make sure the files you attach to your Sakai assignment are the files you intend. Use the steps below to verify your assignment before submission.

Attach the files:

Save Draft. You can use “Save Draft” if you have more work to do.
Preview. When you have attached all the files, select “Proceed”, which takes you to a preview of the submission:

Verify. From this page you can download each attachment. Open each file locally to verify that the file attached to Sakai is the file you intend to submit.




Simple Output
For the first few exercises, your program does not need to format its output. Instead, rely on MATLAB’s default behavior: when a statement does not end with a semicolon (;), MATLAB displays the result in the Command Window. When a semicolon is present, the result is computed but not shown. For example, if you run penny.m from the command window, you should see something like this:
>> penny

t =

    8.8134

v =

   86.4594

>>

title: Assignment 1: Models and Scripts
text:
Problem 1: Penny
Write a script named penny.m to solve Textbook Exercise 1.1.
Notes:

Use Save As in the Live Editor and confirm the file type is set to MATLAB Live Code File (UTF-8) (*.m).
It is good engineering practice to include comments with a description and units. I typically do this by including the units in square brackets, for example:
% Time [s]
t = ...

title: Assignment 1: Models and Scripts
text:
Problem 2: Penny Revisited
Write a script named pennywithair.m to solve Textbook Exercise 1.2.
To explore the functionality of MATLAB’s live code format, include at least the following elements:

Two text blocks and two code blocks
Text formats: Title and Normal
Text items: at least one Equation

See MATLAB’s Format Text in Live Editor.
Hint: you may want to work out the mechanics of this problem first (define the model with pencil and paper) before implementing it in MATLAB. Here is an outline of the calculation.

Write an expression for how long it takes an object under constant acceleration, with no air resistance, to reach a speed of \(v_\text{term} = 18\) m/s.
In that amount of time, how far does the object fall?
How much distance is left to fall before it hits the sidewalk?
How long does it take to travel that distance at a constant speed of \(v_\text{term}\)?

Tip: the keyboard shortcut (Ctrl+Enter or Alt+Enter) for toggling between text and code blocks is convenient.

title: Assignment 1: Models and Scripts
text:
Problem 3: Bike Share
Write a script named bike_update.m to solve Textbook Exercise 2.2.
Again, it is often worthwhile to write out the model (what you are trying to do) before starting the computational implementation (how you are going to solve it).

title: Assignment 1: Models and Scripts
text:
Problem 4: Fluid Statics
Write a script named aquarium.m to demonstrate a parameterized solution to the following statics problem from Engineering Statics. The goal of this exercise is to use MATLAB to implement the calculations associated with this statics problem. The problem and the solution are given, so you do not need to solve (or even understand) the statics problem; just use MATLAB as a calculator to implement the given solution.
An aquarium tank has a window AB for viewing the inhabitants. The width of the window is fixed at \(w = 1.5\) m. The top of the window is shown as 2 m below the surface, but should be parameterized as the variable a. The height of the window is shown as 3 m, but should be considered variable b. The tank contains water with a density of \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m3.

Here is the solution:

(Problem and solution from Engineering Statics: Open and Interactive, Baker and Haynes, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.)
Implement this demonstration as a live script, using alternating text and code blocks to illustrate the steps as shown in the solution above. Test your implementation by defining the input variables as
% Depth of the top of the window: distance from water surface to A in the diagram
a = 2.0;

% Height of the window: distance from A to B in the diagram.
b = 3.0;
Verify that you get the same solution as provided in the example.

Submit and Verify
Submit your programs as separate files with the .m extension. Double-check all case-sensitive file names to make sure they are identical to the file names given in the exercises. See the submission process above.

title: Installing MATLAB
text:
Release
It is highly recommended that you install Release 2026b of MATLAB and Simulink. Release 2025b or higher is required.
It helps with debugging if everyone in the class is using the latest release.

The online documentation from MathWorks is for the latest release, so older releases can behave differently from the documentation you find online.
There are subtle gotchas that make code that works in one release problematic in another. For example, prior to R2024a, local functions had to be at the bottom of the file; see the release notes. Release-dependent bugs like this can be infuriating and can be avoided by using the latest release.

title: Installing MATLAB
text:

MATLAB and Simulink products (toolboxes) are offered à la carte. The NPS license gives you access to all the toolboxes, but installing them all is overkill. Here are the requirements and recommendations. You can re-run the installer to add tools to your install if you find you are missing capabilities.

title: Assignments
text:
Assignment Evaluation Framework

Intent
Assignments in this course are designed to build confidence and competence in applying programming to engineering problem solving. Each assignment includes several exercises, but only one representative exercise is graded for evaluation.
The primary goal is to encourage consistent engagement and improvement, not to penalize small mistakes. Grading emphasizes understanding, effort, and clarity of communication. Students who complete the work thoughtfully and demonstrate learning will typically earn A or B grades.


Grading rubric for the selected exercise










Criterion
Weight
A (Excellent)
B (Satisfactory)
Incomplete




Problem understanding and approach
25%
Shows a clear understanding of the problem and applies an appropriate, well-reasoned method.
Demonstrates general understanding; approach is reasonable but may not be the most efficient or fully explained.
Misinterprets or only partially addresses the problem.


Implementation and code quality
35%
Code runs correctly or nearly correctly; organized, readable, and follows MATLAB conventions.
Code mostly works; minor syntax or logic errors but demonstrates solid effort and structure.
Code incomplete or largely incorrect; intent unclear.


Testing and debugging effort
20%
Demonstrates testing or checking of results; identifies or discusses potential issues.
Some checking or validation attempted, though not systematic.
No evidence of checking, testing, or debugging.


Presentation and communication
20%
Output and plots are clear, labeled, and briefly explained following engineering conventions.
Output mostly clear; minor labeling or explanation issues.
Output unclear or missing explanation.





Grade scale (mastery-focused)



Score
Grade
Meaning




90–100
A
Excellent mastery and presentation


80–89
B
Proficient understanding with minor issues


below 80
Feedback only
Encouraged to discuss or revise





Summary
This grading approach:

Rewards consistent effort and steady improvement.
Encourages sound engineering habits: testing, verification, and clear communication.
Keeps grading meaningful while reducing performance pressure.
Ensures every assignment contributes to the development of practical programming competence.

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
text:
Course Catalog Description
This course offers an introduction to computer system operations and program development using NPS computer facilities. The main goal of the course is to provide an overview of different structured programming techniques, along with an introduction to MATLAB/Simulink/GUIDE, and to use modeling as a tool for scientific and engineering applications. The course discusses the accuracy of digital computations, ways to incorporate symbolic computations, and presents numerical methods in MATLAB functions.

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
text:
Learning Objectives
As a result of successfully finishing this course you should be able to:
Knowledge

Apply the generic concepts of programming (loops, conditionals, functions, data types, and so on) to computational problem solving.
Evaluate alternative computational approaches and make appropriate trade-offs in selecting methods.

Skills

Use the programming capabilities of MATLAB to solve engineering problems with computational techniques.
Present graphical and textual results from computation clearly, following engineering conventions.
Apply debugging and testing techniques to improve and verify computations.
Use MATLAB capabilities (functions, toolboxes, external code) to solve domain-specific problems.

Attitudes

Approach “programming” as a set of tools to be used in solving engineering problems.
Internalize the concepts of modeling as fundamental to the practice of engineering.
Be constructively skeptical of computational solutions and devise tests to improve confidence in solutions.

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
text:
Assignments and Grading
The course deliverables are weekly assignments to be completed individually. There will be nominally nine assignments. These assignments, weighted equally, account for 90% of your course grade. The remaining 10% of the course grade is based on class participation.
If you successfully complete all the assignments on time, your grade will reflect that success. See the Assignment Evaluation Framework for how each assignment is graded.

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
text:
Late Work
Credit for work submitted past the announced deadline will be reduced by 10% per day (or portion of a day) up to 50%. Work will not be accepted more than 5 days late. Deadline extensions will not be granted within 24 hours of assignment deadlines without extenuating circumstances. If there are conflicts with deadlines, please notify the instructor so that other arrangements can be made.

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
section: Collaboration and Use of Generative AI
text:
Collaboration and Use of Generative AI
The goal of this policy is to encourage meaningful learning and prevent activities that hinder your educational development.
Our guiding principle for academic honesty is: “be reasonable.” You are encouraged to collaborate thoughtfully, both with classmates and generative AI tools, but only to the extent that it aids your learning without compromising your individual work. Your submitted assignments must be your own work. In this course, learning comes through practice, including debugging on your own. Frustration can be a valuable part of the learning process: “every moment of frustration is a sign you’re learning something new.”
We view working with other people and using generative AI tools similarly: both are valuable resources that can enhance your learning when used properly. However, they must be used responsibly to support, rather than undermine, your educational growth.
Below are examples (not exhaustive) of what constitutes acceptable and unacceptable collaboration. If unsure, always seek approval from the instructor before proceeding.







Reasonable
Not Reasonable




Discussing ideas and concepts with classmates or an AI tool to enhance understanding.
Sharing code with others, either directly or through an AI tool.


Collaborating with classmates on pseudocode or diagrams without sharing actual code.
Using AI tools to develop or refine actual code instead of doing it yourself.


Asking an AI tool to explain concepts or programming techniques.
Asking a classmate or AI tool to provide solutions or answers to assignments.


Seeking external resources for clarification or technical troubleshooting (not for outright solutions).
Searching for or using online solutions to assessments.


Providing or receiving conceptual help on assignments (not code-specific).
Dividing an assignment and combining work with another student.


Using a few lines of code found online, provided they are not solutions to the assignment, and citing them.
Submitting code found online or from others as your own, without proper citation.


Assisting classmates by discussing debugging techniques without directly sharing code. “Looking over the shoulder” of a classmate to identify and fix bugs.
Sharing or receiving code to solve bugs or complete an assignment.


Reviewing general concepts or strategies from prior offerings to aid your understanding.
Using solutions, code, or completed assignments from prior offerings of the course to complete your own work, even if modified.


Reviewing general study guides or topics covered in past exams to inform your study approach.
Accessing or using previous exams, quizzes, or their solutions (if not explicitly provided in this course) to prepare for current assessments.



In all cases, any external code or ideas incorporated must be cited in your code comments, respecting academic integrity.
Attribution: this policy borrows from many other course policies, including Harvard’s CS50 and USNA’s IC210.

NPS Honor Code and Academic Integrity
The NPS Student Information Handbook in “Section 218: Academic Honor Code” clearly establishes that “Students must follow the Academic Honor Code (NPS instruction 5370.4 series) at all times. The highest standards of honesty and integrity are expected of all students. Plagiarism, fraud, cheating, and verbal or written misrepresentation, constitute a violation of the Academic Honor Code.”

title: Syllabus and Course Policies
text:
Generative AI and Academic Integrity
NPS policy encourages you to explore generative AI tools, and you must use them ethically and responsibly. Your coursework must accurately represent your underlying work, knowledge, and ideas, not the capabilities of an AI tool. If you use generative AI tools, state how you did so and describe how you remained in control of decisions and verification of information. Carefully read the NPS Interim Guiding Principles for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools. Never input classified or controlled unclassified information into a generative AI tool unless the platform has been explicitly approved by DoD or DON CIO for such use.
